Shanghai Jing'an Temple Travel Guide: What to See and Do
 Written by
 Carper
 Updated Sep. 22, 2026 
Jing'an Temple is one of Shanghai's most recognizable contrasts: a gilded Buddhist temple standing amidst a modern city with heavy traffic and beside one of the city's busiest metro stations.
If you only want Shanghai's classic temple-and-skyscraper photograph, you do not need to buy a ticket for Jing'an Temple. The exterior, nearby plaza, and surrounding streets already give you the city contrast most visitors come for.
Pay to enter only if you want to see the temple as a working Buddhist site: incense, worshippers, timber halls, and Buddhist statues at close range. That is the real choice to make before you arrive.
Is Jing'an Temple Worth Paying to Enter?
Jing'an Temple, Shanghai
Opening hours: 7:30–17:00
Entrance fees: 50 RMB/pp (free admission for seniors aged 70 and over and children under 1.3 meters in height)
Time needed: 1–2 hours
For a first visit, think of Jing'an Temple in two parts:
Exterior visit: free, flexible, and best for the iconic "golden temple in modern Shanghai" image.
Inside visit: paid admission, active worship spaces, and a closer look at the halls, statues, and ritual atmosphere.
Skip It If You Only Want a Quick Photo
The exterior is enough for a strong photograph. You can frame the golden roof with skyscrapers, moving traffic, or people crossing the plaza, creating a picture that says "Shanghai" rather than simply recording a temple facade.
Three nearby viewpoints work particularly well:
1. The pedestrian overpass at Huashan Road and Yan'an West Road gives you the widest city composition. From above, place the temple in the distance and let the traffic and towers fill the foreground. Use the railing only as a compositional line; do not climb it or obstruct pedestrians.
2. The reflecting pool near Exit 14 of Jing'an Temple Station works best when the water is still. Hold your phone low and include both the gold roof and its reflection. This is a simple, social-media-friendly shot that needs no ticket.
3. Jing'an Temple Plaza is better for a closer family or couple photograph. Step slightly away from the entrance flow, keep the guardian lions or roofline in the frame, and avoid blocking people who are arriving to worship.
Night view of Jing'an Temple, Shanghai
For daylight, the temple roof usually reads most clearly when the sky is bright.
For a darker, more cinematic image, arrive around sunset. However, to photograph the temple illuminated at night, you will need to visit between 6:00 PM and 10:00 PM on a Friday or Saturday.
If photography is your priority, a China Highlights guide can place these viewpoints into your walking route instead of sending you inside simply because the temple appears on a standard sightseeing list.
5-Day Shanghai, Hangzhou and Suzhou Explore the Elegant China
Enter If You Want to See an Active Buddhist Temple
A close-up look at the architectural details of Shanghai's Jing'an Temple.
Inside, Jing'an Temple makes sense when you want to understand it as an active Buddhist temple rather than a photogenic building.
You may see people lighting incense, praying, and moving quietly through the halls. Keep your voice low, follow signs and staff instructions, and never photograph worshippers, monks, or sacred objects without permission.
Touring the temple usually takes about one hour for the main spaces. With children, or if you want time to observe the architecture, allow longer. If your Shanghai schedule is already packed, the exterior is the better choice.
Mahavira Hall
The Mahavira Hall is the main focus of most visits. It houses a colossal silver statue of Sakyamuni Buddha—standing approximately 8.8 meters tall and weighing around 15 tons—which serves as the temple's most prized treasure.
Worshippers come here to pay their respects and pray for their families' safety and well-being, seeking to avert misfortune and clear away life's troubles and obstacles.
Jade Buddha Hall and Guanyin Hall
The side halls offer a more intimate contrast to the main hall's scale, named for a large white-jade Buddha and a Guanyin statue carved from camphor wood.
These details are best appreciated slowly. Look at the material texture, the expressions on the statues, and the relationship between the statues and the surrounding woodwork.
Worshippers typically visit the Guanyin Hall to pray for harmony in their personal relationships, while seeking physical health and the purification of karmic obstacles at the Jade Buddha Hall.
Jing'an Vajrasana Pagoda
Located in the northwest corner of the temple complex, this seven-story square pagoda is another important part of the temple's skyline.
Beyond admiring its architectural beauty, you may also join the faithful in circumambulating the pagoda three times in a clockwise direction to pray for smooth endeavors and family harmony.
Etiquette for Visitors
Please dress modestly when entering the temple;
Step over the threshold rather than stepping on it;
Light incense with your left hand; do not blow out the flame with your mouth—extinguish it by gently waving the stick instead;
Please speak in a low voice while inside the halls;
Do not block the pathways leading to the altars or incense burners;
Do not photograph Buddha statues, monks, or worshippers without permission.
9-Day Beijing ,Xian and Shanghai Tour China Family Classic Tour 
How Long Do You Need at Jing'an Temple?
30–45 minutes: exterior views and photography;
About 1 hour: a basic inside visit covering the main halls and atmosphere;
1–2 hours: a slower visit with children, photography, or more time for observation.
Jing'an Temple is close to its metro station, but the practical visit still includes reaching the entrance, dealing with tickets, and moving through a busy area.
Avoid scheduling an inside visit immediately before a timed reservation elsewhere.
4-Day Shanghai Family Disneyland Tour 
How to Fit Jing'an Temple into a Shanghai 1-Day Itinerary
Jing'an Temple, Shanghai
Jing'an Temple works well in a fast-paced route that shows several sides of Shanghai in one day: classical gardens, leafy historic streets, a modern business district, and the Bund after dark.
This itinerary is possible, but it is full. Treat the time suggestions as a framework rather than a promise.
Morning: Yu Garden and Yu Garden Bazaar (Enter as early as your ticket and opening arrangements allow, then leave time to browse the surrounding lanes and shops.)
Early afternoon: Wukang Road and Anfu Road (no need to cover every side street. The purpose of this stop is to experience the quieter version of Shanghai.)
Late afternoon: Jing'an Temple and the Shanghai CBD (Visit the exterior first. If you have checked the day's ticket information and have at least an hour available, go inside; otherwise, use the plaza and one nearby viewpoint for the temple-and-city contrast.)
Evening: The Bund at Sunset (This final stop is best kept flexible. Traffic can be slow, and sunset time changes throughout the year. )
This 1-day itinerary gives you a memorable overview of Shanghai, but it does not leave much room for long meals, shopping, or spontaneous stops. If you have 2 or more days in Shanghai, it is better to spread these areas across a slower private itinerary.
A China Highlights travel advisor can help separate the old city, Former French Concession neighborhoods, Jing'an and the Bund into a route with more time for meals, rest and local experiences.

Jade Buddha Temple, Shanghai: What to See and How to Visit
 Written by
 Carper
 Updated Sep. 24, 2026 
Jade Buddha Temple was built around 1918 in the style of the Song Dynasty (960-1279). Named for its 1.9-meter-high white jade Buddha, Jade Buddha Temple is worth about 1–1.5 hours if you want to see the temple's most prized treasure and experience an active Buddhist temple.
If you are on a tight schedule, or your priority is the Bund, Shanghai's old neighborhoods, or the city's modern skyline, you can skip it.
Visit it if you want:
to see Shanghai's famous jade Buddhas;
to experience an active Buddhist temple;
to learn more about Chinese Buddhist culture;
or to spend some time with traditional temple architecture.
Skip it if you want:
Shanghai's skyline and modern cityscape;
old neighborhoods and cafés;
or a very short list of the city's highest-priority sights.
What to See Inside Jade Buddha Temple
Jade Buddha Temple
Address: 170 Anyuan Road, Putuo District, Shanghai
Opening hours: 8:00–16:30 on regular days
Admission: Free
Metro: Line 13, Jiangning Road Station, Exit 3
Walk from the station: About 5 minutes
Recommended visit: 1–1.5 hours
1. The Two Jade Buddhas: The Absolute Must-see
The white jade Buddha of Jade Buddha Temple
The temple is named after two white jade Buddhas brought to Shanghai from Myanmar in the late 19th century.
The most important stop is the Jade Buddha Hall, where you can see the seated jade Buddha, about 1.9 meters high. Then continue to the Reclining Buddha Hall to see the smaller reclining jade Buddha, which represents the Buddha before entering nirvana.
If you only have one hour, prioritize these two halls. You don't need to inspect every hall or Buddhist statue to understand why the temple is significant.
2. Traditional Chinese Temple Architecture
Roof decorations of the Jade Buddha Temple
The jade Buddhas are the main attraction, but the temple itself is also worth noticing.
As you walk through the complex, look for the symmetrical layout, yellow walls, traditional rooflines, courtyards, and carved decorative details.
The architecture gives you a very different side of Shanghai from the skyscrapers around the Bund and Lujiazui.
If you enjoy Chinese architecture, allow a little extra time to walk rather than rushing directly from one Buddha hall to the next.
Photography Tips
If you want photos, focus on the architecture, courtyards, roof details, and overall temple atmosphere rather than trying to photograph every hall.
Photography is restricted in certain worship areas or during religious activities. Follow the signs inside the temple.
3. Taste the Vegetarian Cuisine
The temple also has a vegetarian food section serving traditional Buddhist vegetarian dishes with Shanghai-style cooking (priced at 50–70 RMB per person).
This works well for vegans, or if you want to eat immediately after visiting rather than finding another restaurant.
I would treat the vegetarian food as an optional add-on, not the main reason to visit. Come for the jade Buddhas first.
Check detailed information on its official website: Jade Buddha Temple.
5-Day Shanghai, Hangzhou and Suzhou Explore the Elegant China
How Much Time Do You Need at Jade Buddha Temple?
Koi Pond at the Jade Buddha Temple
Less than 1 hour: See the two jade Buddhas, look around the main halls, and leave.
1–2 hours: See the two Buddhas, explore the main architectural spaces, and spend some time observing the temple atmosphere. This is the amount of time we would suggest for most travelers.
2–3 hours: Worth considering if you have a strong interest in Buddhism, Chinese temple architecture, religious culture, or an interest in having a vegan meal inside.
If you are visiting Shanghai for only one or two days and Buddhist culture is not a priority, don't force Jade Buddha Temple into your itinerary simply because it is famous.
The time may be better spent on the Bund, the Former French Concession, or another experience that matches your interests more closely.
If you're unsure whether it deserves a place in your short Shanghai itinerary, tell us how many days you have and what else you want to see. We can help you decide where it fits without adding unnecessary cross-city travel.
8-Day Beijing–Xi'an–Shanghai Tour China Golden Triangle
Jade Buddha Temple vs. Jing'an Temple: Which Fits Your Itinerary?
Shanghai Jing'an Temple night view
 Jade Buddha Temple
 Jing'an Temple
 Main appeal
 Jade Buddhas and Buddhist culture
 Temple architecture + modern Shanghai
 Experience
 Slower and more cultural
 Quicker and more visual
 Suggested time
 1–2 hours
 About 30–60 minutes for a quick photo
 Best for
 Travelers interested in Buddhism and traditional temple culture
 Travelers who want a temple stop without spending much time
Choose Jing'an Temple for a quick architectural stop, while opting for Jade Buddha Temple if you want to spend more time understanding Buddhist culture and seeing the famous jade Buddhas.
You don't need to visit both unless temples are a specific interest.
5-Day Shanghai and Hangzhou High Tech Tour 
How to Fit Jade Buddha Temple into Your Shanghai Itinerary
Jade Buddha Temple works best as one stop within a Former French Concession route, rather than as a destination that requires a special trip across Shanghai.
For example, you could visit the Former French Concession in the morning, have lunch nearby, and then continue to Jade Buddha Temple for a cultural immersion.
If your Shanghai itinerary is already full, don't add the temple just to collect another famous attraction.
If you want to visit Jade Buddha Temple without wasting time crossing Shanghai, we can build it into your private sightseeing route and combine it with nearby experiences that match your interests.

Zhujiajiao Water Town: How to See Its Less Touristy Side
 Written by
 Carper
 Updated Sep. 10, 2026 
If you have only 1–2 days in Shanghai, skip Zhujiajiao and focus on the Bund, Yu Garden, the Former French Concession, and the city's skyline.
But if you have 3 days or more, Zhujiajiao is worth a half-day, especially if you want a slower contrast to central Shanghai.
The trick is to avoid spending your whole visit on the main canal streets. Give yourself 3–4 hours to mix residential lanes, old gardens, stone bridges, and quiet canal views.
Is Zhujiajiao Worth Half a Day?
Zhujiajiao Less-touristy Route
Should You Take a Boat in Zhujiajiao?
Is Zhujiajiao Suitable for Children and Older Travelers?
When Is the Best Time to Visit Zhujiajiao
How to Get to Zhujiajiao
Is Zhujiajiao Worth Half a Day?
Zhujiajiao Water Town in summer season
Our picks:
1–2 days in Shanghai: Skip Zhujiajiao.
3 days: Optional. Go if you have already covered the main sights and want a slower half-day outside central Shanghai.
4+ days: Recommended. You have enough time to add Zhujiajiao without taking time away from Shanghai's major sights.
Yes, Zhujiajiao is a real historic town. If you want to experience a Jiangnan water town without leaving Shanghai for a full day, this is it.
However, it is not an untouched village. The main streets have souvenir shops, snack stalls, restaurants, boat rides, and plenty of visitors. That means your experience depends heavily on when you arrive and where you walk.
If you arrive on a weekday around 8:30–9:00 AM, you can start with quieter residential lanes before the busiest part of the town fills up.
If you only have one full day in Shanghai, this journey to the western suburbs is not the best use of your time.
Unsure whether Zhujiajiao fits your Shanghai itinerary? We can help you compare it with Suzhou, Hangzhou, or another water town before you give up half a day of your trip.
The Best Zhujiajiao Half-Day Route: See the Town, Not Just the Tourist Street
Route: Visitor Center → West Well Street (西井街) → Kezhi Garden (课植园) & Hexin Garden (和心园) → Fangsheng Bridge (放生桥) → Jiangnan First Tea House (江南第一茶楼) → Tai'an Bridge (泰安桥) → Lang Bridge (廊桥) → City God Temple (城隍庙) → Daqing Post Office (大清邮局)
Distance: Roughly 4–5 km (around 7,000–9,000 steps)
Time needed: About 3–4 hours at a relaxed pace
Don't try to turn it into a checklist. The quieter lanes between the landmarks are part of the experience, rather than being hurried from one crowded photo spot to another.
1. Start at West Well Street, Not Fangsheng Bridge
Alleys of the Zhujiajiao Water Town, Shanghai
When you arrive at the visitor center, don't immediately follow the crowd toward the main canal and Fangsheng Bridge.
Turn into West Well Street (西井街) first.
The atmosphere changes quickly. Instead of souvenir shops and tour groups, you'll see residential lanes, older houses, local shops, and people going about their daily routines.
If you have another 30–45 minutes, continue toward East Well Street (东井街). It is a useful extension when you want more residential scenery rather than another landmark.
2. Don't Skip the Gardens: Both Are Worth Visiting
Kezhi Garde in Zhujiajiao Water Town
The canals and bridges show you the postcard side of the town. Kezhi Garden and Hexin Garden show you how wealthy local families actually lived and how Jiangnan garden design worked. They are also a good way to step away from the busiest commercial streets.
Current prices are:
Kezhi Garden: ¥20
Hexin Garden: ¥30
Shanghai Helong Art Gallery: ¥20
Three-attraction joint ticket: ¥60
Kezhi Garden (课植园) is the larger of the two, with more space to explore and a mix of traditional Jiangnan garden design and Western-style architectural elements.
Hexin Garden (和心园) is smaller but more intimate, with its own gardens, historic buildings, and collections.
We recommend both rather than choosing between them. They are different enough that visiting one does not make the other feel repetitive, and together they give you a much better sense of Zhujiajiao beyond its canals and tourist streets.
The paid attractions are open 8:30 AM–5:00 PM. If you buy the ¥60 joint ticket online, you need to exchange it for a physical ticket by 3:00 PM.
For this route, visit the gardens before Fangsheng Bridge. That way, you see the quieter historic side first and leave the busiest canal area for the classic views later.
3. Walk to Fangsheng Bridge for the Classic Zhujiajiao View
Fangsheng Bridge in Zhujiajiao Water Town
Now head toward Fangsheng Bridge (放生桥).
Built in 1571, it is one of Zhujiajiao's defining landmarks and the town's classic viewpoint over the canal.
This is where the water-town image you've probably seen online starts to make sense: stone bridge, whitewashed houses, narrow waterways, willow trees, and wooden boats moving below.
Expect this area to be considerably busier than the residential lanes, which is totally acceptable.
You don't come here to avoid people completely—you come here for the view.
8-Day Shanghai, Hangzhou, Suzhou Family TourShanghai-Hangzhou-Wuzhen-Suzhou 
4. Stop at Jiangnan First Tea House
The Jiangnan First Tea House
After roughly 1½–2 hours of walking, take a proper break.
The Jiangnan First Tea House (江南第一茶楼) sits beside the water and makes a useful 20–30 minute pause.
Order tea, sit by the canal, and watch the boats rather than rushing straight to the next attraction.
This is one of the moments when Zhujiajiao works best: you stop sightseeing and simply watch the town move around you.
5. Cross Tai'an Bridge and Lang Bridge
Lang Bridge in Zhujiajiao Water Town
Continue toward Tai'an Bridge (泰安桥) and then Lang Bridge (廊桥).
Tai'an Bridge is where you'll find the large characters "朱家角" (Zhujiajiao) painted on a wall—the classic spot that signals you've arrived. 
Lang Bridge is a particularly good photo stop because you can frame the canal, old buildings, stone bridges, and wooden boats in one view.
If photography matters to you, this section is more rewarding than trying to collect every bridge in town.
6. Finish at City God Temple and Daqing Post Office
City God Temple in Zhujiajiao Water Town
The City God Temple (城隍庙) is a small stop rather than a major attraction. Give it 10–15 minutes if you enjoy historic religious architecture and quieter courtyards.
Then continue to Daqing Post Office (大清邮局).
This restored Qing-era post office is an easy final stop. You can buy a postcard, have it stamped with a Zhujiajiao postmark, and continue walking without adding much time to your route.
Should You Take a Boat: Treat It as an Add-On, Not a Must
Taking a boat tour at Zhujiajiao Water Town
Our recommendation:
Solo/couple: Walk first; add a boat only if the water experience is important to you.
Family/group of 4–6: A private hand-rowed boat makes more sense.
Already/plan to visit Suzhou/Hangzhou/Guilin: The walking route may give you more variety than another short water-town boat ride.
The boat ride is not a bad experience. It is simply not essential for everyone.
The current official hand-rowed boat routes cost ¥200–300 per boat, with a maximum of 6 passengers, and take about 15–20 minutes.
For a family or group of up to six, the price becomes much easier to justify because you are paying by boat rather than per person.
For a solo traveler or couple, it is a different calculation. It depends on whether you want to charter the boat alone or share it with others.
Instead of spending hours lining up for a 15-minute experience, you may get more value from standing on Fangsheng Bridge or Lang Bridge, where you can see the boats, canals, bridges, and old houses together rather than viewing the scenery from inside a short boat ride.
4-Day Shanghai Family Disneyland Tour 
Is Zhujiajiao Suitable for Children and Older Travelers?
Yes, with one important warning: the streets are mostly manageable, but the stone bridges can be steep and uneven.
For a slower family visit, stay mainly around: West Well Street → central canal → Fangsheng Bridge → tea house
You do not need to climb every bridge or visit every attraction. For older travelers or anyone with limited mobility, a private transfer can also remove the unnecessary walking between the metro station and the old town.
If you're traveling with children or older family members, we can adjust the route to reduce unnecessary walking while keeping the most photogenic canal and bridge views.
When Is the Best Time to Visit Zhujiajiao: Weekday Morning Beats Weekend Crowds
For the best chance of a quieter experience, arrive around 8:30–9:00 AM on a weekday.
Start with West Well Street and the residential lanes while the town is still relatively calm.
By late morning, the main tourist streets become noticeably busier, particularly on weekends and public holidays.
If you cannot arrive in the morning, arriving after 3:00 PM can give you quieter streets and a different atmosphere. 
But there is a trade-off: the paid attractions close around 5:00 PM, and you may not have enough time to see them all. So a late arrival is better for atmosphere than for sightseeing.
5-Day Shanghai and Hangzhou High Tech Tour 
How to Get to Zhujiajiao: Metro for Value, Private Transfer for Comfort
Metro Line 17: Best for budget travelers. Take Metro Line 17 to Zhujiajiao Station, and use the local scenic shuttle to the visitor center, or walk toward the old town.
Taxi or ride-hailing: Easier for small groups. This is more convenient when you are traveling with children, luggage, or several people. You avoid the transfer from the metro station and arrive closer to the old town.
Private transfer: Best when Zhujiajiao is part of a full Shanghai day. A private transfer becomes worthwhile when you want to combine Zhujiajiao with another Shanghai experience.
Private transfer is particularly useful for families or older travelers who would rather spend their limited sightseeing time walking through Zhujiajiao than navigating public transport.
If you don't want to spend part of your Shanghai day figuring out transfers, we can arrange a private tour and fit Zhujiajiao into your existing Shanghai itinerary.

How to Plan a Trip to Shanghai Without Rushing Between Spots
 Written by
 Carper
 Updated Jul. 20, 2026 
For most first-timers, Shanghai is often the first or last stop on a China trip. However, many still aren't sure how to actually "use" the city in their itinerary.
If you only have two or three days in Shanghai, it's tempting to squeeze every famous attraction into your itinerary. That's also why many first-time visitors leave feeling they spent more time crossing the city than enjoying it.
The easiest way to explore Shanghai is to plan each day around one part of the city instead of a checklist of sights.
You'll still see Shanghai's highlights, but you'll also have time to enjoy the cafés, local food, riverside walks, and neighborhoods that make the city memorable.
Why You Should Plan by Neighborhood
How Many Days Do You Really Need?
How to Spend Each Day
Best Areas to Stay in Shanghai
The Best Time to Visit
FAQs
Why You Should Plan by Neighborhood, Not Attractions
To truly experience Shanghai, walking is an unavoidable part of the experience.
Remember one thing before planning your days in Shanghai: the quality of your trip will depend less on how many places you visit, and more on how little you move between different parts of the city.
Shanghai is vast, and its highlights are scattered across districts. Most first-timers try to squeeze the Bund, the Former French Concession, and Shanghai Tower, which are from three distinct districts, into a single day, which makes chasing must-see sights feel exhausting.
Try planning your days by neighborhood. To truly feel the city, it's better to dedicate a half-day or full day to only one district, exploring its sights and its unexpected corners all in one go.
For example, combining the Bund, Nanjing Road, and Yu Garden in the same day gives you a walkable itinerary in Huangpu District, with a flexible pace and deeper experience.
This approach respects the city's scale and rewards you with surprises that no guidebook mentions—hidden courtyards, laid-back locals, and quaint little stalls that you would never spot from a taxi window.
Your days in Shanghai should not just be about sightseeing. They should be about truly experiencing the city, one neighbourhood at a time.
8-Day Beijing–Xi'an–Shanghai Tour China Golden Triangle
How Many Days Do You Really Need?
Shanghai is a city that rewards time, but it is also remarkably accommodating to shorter stays. Not all attractions are created equal, and knowing the real time commitment helps you plan realistically.
A 3-day stay is our most recommended; it balances visiting major attractions with a leisurely sightseeing pace. However, the right length depends entirely on your travel style and what you hope to take away from the trip.
2 Days: Focus On the Classic Core
If you really don't have time to see the Bund at night, then taking a walk during the day is also a great option.
Two days are okay for a quick stopover, a brief first warm-up on a trip to China, or a relaxed final stop.
With this timeframe, you should focus exclusively on the classic core: the Bund, Nanjing Road, the Yu Garden, and the Pudong skyline. This is a highlight reel, not a deep dive, which is perfectly fine for a first taste.
You can easily cover all these Shanghai's greatest hits without feeling rushed, if only you stay disciplined and resist the urge to add "just one more" attraction.
3 Days: The Sweet Spot for First-Timers
Three days is the most commonly recommended length for first-time visitors, giving you enough room to see the major landmarks without rushing, while also allowing for one slower day.
The classic three-day structure looks like this: two days for the core sights (the Bund, Nanjing Road, Yu Garden, and Pudong Skyline), and one full day dedicated to the Former French Concession.
This third day is where the magic happens.
No need to be rushed to ticket booths or squeeze yourself into the observation decks; just enjoy a walk along leafy streets, hopping café stops, and the kind of unhurried wandering that makes a city feel like your own.
If you appreciate the charm of classic Chinese water towns, you might consider skipping the strolls through the Former French Concession and instead visiting Zhujiajiao or Tongli water towns to admire the classical aesthetics of Jiangnan.
4－5 Days: Explore the Complete Shanghai, or Its Nearby Cities
Experience traditional Chinese water town by taking a boat tour in Zhujiajiao.
For most travelers, four to five days is the ideal length to plan a trip with a higher tolerance for emergencies.
You can tick off the classics, spend a full day in the Former French Concession, or add a detour, whether that is Disneyland, a day trip to a water town like Zhujiajiao, or simply revisiting a neighborhood you liked, and still have a buffer day.
Don't underestimate the extra day that gives you weather flexibility and room to rest. Shanghai is a walking city, and fatigue is real.
With four or five days, you never have to choose between seeing something and catching your breath. You can do both.
Still deciding how long to spend in Shanghai? We can help you balance Shanghai with destinations like Suzhou, Hangzhou, or Beijing based on your interests instead of following a fixed route.
8-Day Shanghai, Hangzhou, Suzhou Family TourShanghai-Hangzhou-Wuzhen-Suzhou 
How to Spend Each Day Without Crossing the City
Shanghai's attractions are clustered into distinct neighborhoods.
For a smooth and leisurely pace, try your best to dedicate each day to only one area and explore it thoroughly, letting the neighborhood itself become the experience rather than a collection of disconnected stops.
Day 1: The Bund & Huangpu Core
Begin your day at the historic heart of Shanghai, the Bund, arrive before 8:30 AM if you want to see locals exercising and photograph the skyline without tour groups.
You can enjoy a quiet walk along the riverbank, taking in the colonial-era architecture on one side and the futuristic Pudong skyline on the other. By around 9:30 AM, group tours begin arriving, and the promenade becomes noticeably busier.
From there, walk west into Nanjing Road, one of Shanghai's most famous shopping streets.
Unless shopping is one of your priorities, treat Nanjing Road as the easiest walking route between the Bund and Yu Garden rather than a destination on its own.
In the afternoon, head to Yu Garden and the surrounding City God Temple bazaar. This is Shanghai's remaining side of traditional China, with classical pavilions, winding bridges, and lively street food stalls.
End your day back at the Bund for the spectacular nightly view, when the entire skyline illuminates across the river.
Why this works: This route covers Shanghai's most iconic highlights, with everything reached within walking distance. No taxis, no metro transfers, just a comfortable day of strolling through Shanghai's postcard-like corridors.
Day 2: The French Concession & Jing'an District
Dedicate your second day to Shanghai's most walkable neighborhood.
Start at Wukang Road and the iconic Wukang Building, then wander through the leafy streets of the former French Concession. This area is packed with historic villas, boutique shops, and street-side cafés that feel a world away from the skyscrapers.
Turn north to explore Anfu Road for vintage stores, stop for coffee at a garden café, or a street-front restaurant for lunch.
If time allows, you can visit the nearby Jing'an Temple or Jade Buddha Temple for a Buddhist touch, or the creative hub of Tianzifang for shopping around.
Why this works: The Former French Concession is a self-contained universe of charm. You do not need to leave it to have a full, satisfying day, but just wander, discover, and let the neighborhood reveal itself.
Day 3: Pudong & Modern Shanghai
Cross the river on your third day by ferry to experience Shanghai's futuristic side.
Visit the observation decks of the Shanghai Tower before 9 AM for a much shorter wait than the late-morning peak. Then you can enjoy panoramic views of the city from the highest building in Shanghai.
After taking stunning photos of the Bund skyline by the water, you can add the Shanghai Museum (East Branch) for cultural appreciation, or the DJI Retail Store for high-tech product experiences.
Why this works: Pudong is best experienced as a dedicated day, not squeezed between other districts. The skyline views are the main event, and rushing through them defeats the purpose.
Only Add a Day Trip If You Have Four Days or More
If you have four or five days in Shanghai and want to escape the city, you have several excellent day-trip options. But not every destination suits every traveler. Here is a quick decision guide to help you choose the right one.

 Admire world-class gardens with a 30-min train.

 See the UNESCO West Lake and tea plantations with a 45-min train.

 Dedicate one or half a day to exploring with a direct 2-hour metro.

14-Day Beijing – Xi'an – Zhangjiajie - Guilin/Yangshuo – Shanghai Private Tour China Natural Wonders Discovery 
Best Areas to Stay in Shanghai for First-Time Visitors
The Bund's night skyline is the single most defining image of Shanghai, and is also the biggest factor driving hotel prices. A room with that iconic river view can easily cost three times more than a similar room without it.
For first-time visitors, the smartest choice is to prioritize location over luxury.
The good news is that most of Shanghai's major attractions are concentrated in or around Huangpu District, so you do not need to venture far to stay central. The real question is which flavor of central fits your style.
The Bund: Shanghai's Iconic Waterfront
Staying on the Bund puts you at the heart of Shanghai's historic charm, where colonial-era architecture faces the futuristic Pudong skyline.
Imagine watching the nightly light show after nightfall, and stepping out of your hotel straight to be a part of the scenery is an experience in itself.
The trade-off is simple: you pay for the view, or you walk a few minutes or longer to enjoy it for free.
Hotel Recommendations
Top-tier properties like the Peninsula Shanghai, Waldorf Astoria Shanghai On the Bund, and Bellagio Shanghai deliver relatively unobstructed views, and short access to the city's most photographed stretch.
For a more budget-friendly Bund-adjacent option, Sunrise On The Bund Hotel on the North Bund sits just across the Suzhou Creek and offers walking-distance convenience at a much lower price point.
Pudong CBD: Great For Business Travelers
Across the Huangpu River, Pudong is Shanghai's financial heart, which appeals most to business travelers for its short commute and advanced facilities.
However, for first-time leisure travelers, you may find Pudong a bit plain. The Bund's historic charm is just a cab ride away, but the neighborhood itself lacks the walkable, character-filled streets of the older districts.
Reserve Pudong as a one-night splurge for the view, not as your primary base.
Hotel Recommendations
The Mandarin Oriental, with its riverside views and stunning night skyline, adds a touch of understated luxury.
The J Hotel at Shanghai Tower currently claims the title of the city's highest hotel, offering unparalleled panoramic views on clear days, when you can see the entire city lying beneath you.
The Former French Concession: Charming Streets with A Relaxed Pace
This leafy district offers Shanghai's most walkable and romantic neighborhood.
Tree-lined avenues, historic villas, boutique shops, and hidden cafés define the experience here, making it perfect for travelers with one or two free days to simply wander and explore.
The drawback? You may need to take a taxi or metro to reach the Bund, Nanjing Road, and other major sights. But for many first-timers, the trade-off is totally worth it: you trade the postcard view for a more intimate, local feel.
Hotel Recommendations
The Hengshan Garden Hotel sits near the iconic Wukang Building and Soong May-ling's former residence, with plenty of independent shops and eateries within a ten-minute walk.
Nanjing Road: Highly Commercialized for Shopping Around
Nanjing Road is one of Shanghai's most famous shopping streets, packed with flagship stores and fancy dining options, which makes it incredibly convenient for first-timers.
Staying here puts you right in the middle of the retail action, with the Bund just a fifteen-minute walk away. This could work great for you if shopping is your thing, or you want everything at your doorstep.
However, the crowds can be overwhelming, which makes it less than a relaxing base; hotel prices fluctuate significantly depending on the season, and many properties in this area show their age.
Hotel Recommendations
The most central option is the Shanghai Grand Hotel, while the Shanghai Marriott Marquis City Centre and Conrad Shanghai offer newer, more polished brand experiences.
For something with character, the Yangtze Boutique Shanghai provides a boutique feel in a heritage building, though it comes with the same trade-off of busy surroundings.
The Best Time to Visit Depends on Your Walking Comforts
Shanghai is a walking city. Prepare yourself to spend hours on your feet by strolling the Bund, wandering the Former French Concession, and navigating Yu Garden's winding pathways.
Considering your daily outdoor activities, the weather directly impacts how far you can go and how much you enjoy each day.
The Best Choices: Spring (March–May) and Autumn (September–November)
Cherry Blossom Landscape at Shanghai Postal Museum
Spring and autumn are the clear winners.
Both seasons make long strolls genuinely enjoyable, with mild temperatures around 20°C (68°F) and acceptable humidity averaging 40%.
The only drawback? Drizzles are common, and both have peak travel periods, such as late March to early April in spring and the Chinese National Holiday from Oct 1 to 7, when you can expect more crowds and higher hotel prices.
Clear but Cold: Winter (December–February)
If your main goal is to witness the futuristic Shanghai, winter gives you the clearest views of the Pudong skyline.
This is a great choice if you want lower prices and fewer tourists. But you will need to tolerate the chill since temperatures can drop to 0°C (32°F), and the wind along the Bund bites especially hard.
Remember to dress in thick layers, bring gloves and a woolen hat, so you can still walk comfortably.
Hot and Humid: Summer (June–August)
Summer is the toughest season for a walking trip.
You can expect temperatures that often exceed 35°C (95°F) with oppressive humidity above 90%. Even short walks leave you exhausted and sweaty. Afternoon showers offer little relief, and wear sandals in case wet shoes increase the discomfort.
If summer is your only option, plan your outdoor activities for early morning or late evening to avoid the midday heat, take frequent breaks in air-conditioned spaces, and accept that you will move slower than usual.
5-Day Shanghai and Hangzhou High Tech Tour 
FAQs About Planning a Shanghai Trip
Should Shanghai Be My First or Last Stop in China?
Shanghai works well as either a first or last stop. It all depends on your itinerary and travel style.
As one of China's most international and English-friendly cities, Shanghai can be a great first stop to help you adjust to China's pace and ease into the culture.
If you are traveling through multiple cities, ending in Shanghai gives you a relaxed finale. You can easily get some world-class shopping, great dining, and easy access to the airport for your departure flight from this metropolis.
Is Shanghai Easy for Families With Children?
Yes, Shanghai is surprisingly family-friendly, but there are a few things to keep in mind.
The metro system and main attractions, like the Bund, Yu Garden, and the Shanghai Tower, are stroller-friendly. Teenagers can also have a great time at Shanghai Disneyland, Shanghai Science and Technology Museum, or Shanghai Wild Animal Park.
However, most public restrooms outside high-end shopping malls often lack maternal and child facilities, so remember to bring your own supplies and ask staff for help.
What's more, the midday heat and humidity can be tough on young children, so plan outdoor activities for cooler parts of the day, and use air-conditioned transit for your daily visit.
4-Day Shanghai Family Disneyland Tour 
What's the Best Way to Get Around Shanghai?
For most first-time visitors, the best strategy is a mix of walking and the metro.
Walk within neighborhoods like the Bund and Former French Concession, use the metro to jump between areas, and reserve taxis for when you are tired or carrying bags.
Avoid taxis during rush hour, when traffic can be heavy; the metro can be even quicker, but also very packed.
As for a door-to-door transfer, consider traveling with us at China Highlights. We offer a personalized, no-shopping itinerary, planned according to your interests, that comes with a professional local guide and private transfers for the whole trip.
Is Shanghai Easy Without Speaking Chinese?
Yes, Shanghai is the most English-friendly city in mainland China and is designed to welcome visitors from all over the world as an international metropolis.
Expect signs of the metro system and major attractions to be bilingual in English and Chinese, and hotel staff to use English.
Translation apps, pictures on the menus, and saved addresses in Chinese characters can handle the rest.
You will manage just fine with minimal preparation, like learning a few polite phrases like "xièxiè" (thank you).
Exploring Shanghai with China Highlights
If you'd like to skip the uncertainty of planning and turn your time in Shanghai into a well-paced, fully organized journey, China Highlights can help design a route that fits your travel style, pace, and family needs. 
From choosing the right neighborhoods to balancing sightseeing, food stops, and downtime, every detail can be arranged so you don't have to constantly check maps or rethink your plan on the go.

Shanghai Itinerary Planning Guide: How Many Days Do You Need
 Written by
 Carper
 Updated Aug. 6, 2026 
Most first-time visitors wonder the same thing when planning Shanghai: if adding another day to Shanghai means taking one away from another destination, is it really worth it?
For a rather comprehensive trip, we'd like to recommend having three days in Shanghai, so you will have enough time to experience the city instead of feeling like you're checking off a list.
Instead of completing a mission of moving from one landmark to the next, we would like to take you to unfold the everyday moments that make Shanghai one of the most memorable stops on your first journey in China.
Content Preview
Why a Three-Day Stay in Shanghai
One Day in Shanghai
Two Days in Shanghai
Should You Spend More Than 3 Days in Shanghai?
Why We Strongly Recommend a Three-Day Stay in Shanghai
Most first-time visitors wonder: can't I see Shanghai's highlights in one day? Technically yes, but you may leave feeling like you only saw the cover of the book.
One or two days let you see Shanghai. Three days let you experience it.
We would like to describe Shanghai in three layers:
The historic Bund and old city streets.
The leafy, everyday life of the Former French Concession.
The futuristic energy of Pudong.
Each layer deserves its own day, so you can slow down, wander, and actually feel the contrast between them. 
Follow our three-day plan that takes you through all three layers—one day for the past, one for the present, and one for the future—at a pace that leaves room for discovery, not just checklist-ticking.
Still haven't decided when to visit Shanghai? See Best Times to Visit Shanghai to find the period that suits you the most.
Day 1: A Glimpse Into Shanghai's Past
The International Architecture Exhibition at the Bund, Shanghai
Start your morning on the Bund, walking along the historic waterfront with a guide who will bring the old buildings to life—from the grand Astor House Hotel to the iconic Peace Hotel and the former HSBC Building.
To help you create lasting memories, we offer postcards and stamps for you to choose from, so you can send a piece of the Bund home to someone special.
After lunch near Nanjing Road, continue your day to Yu Garden, a classical Chinese garden hidden in the old city. Wander through its winding corridors, koi ponds, and bizarre rockeries, while learning about the garden's remarkable story of destruction and rebirth.
If time allows, stroll along Shanghai Old Street before returning to the Bund for sunset. We suggest arriving there 30–40 minutes early to claim a good spot on the waterfront and watch the skyline transform as the city lights begin to glow.
6-Day Beijing and Shanghai Tour A Tale of Two Cities 
Day 2: Be a Part of Shanghai's Lively Present
Open-air cafes on Sinan Road in the Former French Concession of Shanghai
Your day begins beneath the plane trees of the Former French Concession. 
Start your walk at Fuxing Park, where a century ago French residents sipped coffee behind iron gates while Chinese locals could only look in from outside. Today, the park is for everyone.
Walk along Sinan Road, lined with vintage villas and quiet doorways, where your guide will share the stories of the families who once lived here. You can pause for a while at a corner café tucked inside a lilong alleyway, where modern coffee shops and bakeries now breathe new life into the old lanes.
If you are curious about Shanghai cuisine, we can arrange a cooking class at a local home—from shopping for ingredients at the market to sitting down to savor the dishes you have made.
End your walk at the Wukang Building, a ship-shaped apartment block that once housed foreign elites and now stands as a beloved landmark of modern Shanghai.
5-Day Shanghai, Hangzhou and Suzhou Explore the Elegant China
Day 3: Jump to Shanghai's Future
The Shanghai Trio at night
Today your trip will start with a ride—an autonomous one—to Shanghai Tower, the world's third-tallest building. 
Take the high-speed elevator to the 118th-floor observation deck, where the daytime panorama reveals the city buzzing with life below: cars like toys, crowds like ants.
Then your guide will lead you to step into the future at the world's first retail store operated by Gal, an embodied intelligent robot. Place your order and watch as the robot handles everything. 
If you have extra time, try ordering a takeaway delivered by drone, which typically arrives within fifteen minutes.
End your day at the DJI or Huawei flagship store, where you can test the latest drones, gadgets, and electric vehicles that are already shaping how people live in Shanghai.
Your right travel length always depends on your travel style and available time.
Of course, you can always swap part of the itinerary for attractions that match your interests, such as Shanghai Disneyland and Zhujiajiao Water Town, but you may inevitably lose some understanding of Shanghai.
Whatever you choose, this guide will help you build an itinerary around what matters most to you, not just what is popular on social media. Shanghai is not a place to rush through, but a city to immerse yourself in.
5-Day Shanghai and Hangzhou High Tech Tour 
One Day in Shanghai: See the Highlights, But Not the Whole Story
A view of the Shanghai skyline during the day
A Typical One-Day Itinerary (Ideal Timeline)
9 AM - 11 AM: Shanghai Tower
12 AM - 1 PM: Yu Garden
1 PM - 2 PM: Lunch Break
3 PM - 4 PM: The Former French Concession (With a limited day trip, you can only visit Wukang Road, and skip Sinan Park and Fuxing Park to miss a deeper understanding of Shanghai's colonial history.)
5 PM - 6 PM: The Bund (We believe the Bund is more worthwhile to spend 2 hours walking around, as you can truly step into the historical buildings and see firsthand what the Chinese have accomplished in this economic center. However, due to the limited time on a day trip, only a simple walk can be well-arranged.)
This itinerary covers four must-see sights with a well-planned schedule, and adding more is simply not feasible. As we have already considered the queues and traffic with a stress-free private transfer, you will be in good hands traveling with us.
For a self-guided day trip, taking a taxi or metro is workable, but you're very likely to encounter traffic jams or overcrowding during midday and afternoon rush hours, which may lead to a delay of subsequent sightseeing.
To enjoy a smooth one-day trip, consider starting your day at 8:00 AM to beat the crowds and avoid rush hours. Alternatively, you can also cut one attraction that you find less appealing for a more relaxed pace.
Looking for a stress-free experience? See our Shanghai Tours.
Two Days in Shanghai: Focus On the Core Sights
Explore the tree-lined Former French Concession of Shanghai
Having two days in Shanghai means you have time to feel the city from two distinct layers, but you still can't afford to squeeze all the highlights or even a side trip from Shanghai city center without sacrificing experiences or the relaxed pace.
The Bund and the Former French Concession, representing the past and lively present, are both excellent candidates for this kind of immersive experience.
On Day One, you can walk the Bund, step inside the grand buildings of the "International Architecture Exhibition," and uncover the stories behind them. After lunch, continue to the old city and Yu Garden—all within walking distance—and return to the Bund before 6 PM for a stunning sunset view of the skyline, if the weather is clear.
On Day Two, immerse yourself in the leafy streets of the Former French Concession. Walk along Sinan Road, pass by the legendary mansions that once belonged to Shanghai's most powerful figures, and stop at Tianzifang's maze-like alleyways, where traditional lilong housing now hosts boutiques, galleries, and cafés.
If you are more interested in the futuristic side of Shanghai, feel free to replace one day that may seem less appealing to you, to enjoy the panoramic views of the urban area from Shanghai Tower's peak and high-tech gadgets at Pudong.
Should You Spend More Than 3 Days in Shanghai?
For most travelers, three days is enough to cover Shanghai's highlights without feeling rushed. But if you have four or five days, you have the luxury of going deeper.
Extra days allow you to hop on Shanghai's galleries, take a day trip to a nearby water town like Zhujiajiao or Tongli, or simply spend an unhurried afternoon in a neighborhood park watching locals go about their daily routines.
Families with children might use an extra day for Shanghai Disneyland, Legoland Shanghai, or the Science and Technology Museum.
Check our 4-Day Shanghai Family Tour with Disneyland.
If Shanghai has satisfied you and you want to explore further, a day trip to Suzhou or Hangzhou is recommended.
We can arrange for your tour guide in Shanghai to travel with you, so you won't have to adjust to a new one and can continue to enjoy a stress-free, relaxing journey.
See our 5-Day Shanghai and Hangzhou Tour for inspiration.

Best/Worst Times to Visit Shanghai 2026: Tips for All Months
 Written by
 Carper
 Updated Apr. 13, 2026 
We're often asked when the best time is to visit Shanghai.
Shanghai has a humid subtropical climate with four distinct seasons, and there's something to enjoy anytime you visit.
The simplest answer: autumn (September to November) is sunny, mild, and dry, and relatively uncrowded. Spring (March to May) is also lovely, though a bit more humid with occasional light rain.
But if you want to avoid the crowds or catch a specific seasonal highlight, a general "best season" answer isn't always enough.
Based on our experience and customer feedback, we've found that timing your trip around specific periods can make a big difference. We'll share those insights below, so you can plan a vacation that's as close to perfect as possible.
Considering your stay in Shanghai may not be too long, you may also want to know how to plan a Shanghai trip that meets your needs and travel length.
Content Preview
Autumn and Spring: Top Choices
Winter: The Cheapest Time
Summer: The Worst Time Without Strategies
Dates to Avoid in 2026/2027
Autumn and Spring: Your Top Choices
Wukang Mansion in Autumn, Shanghai, China
Autumn (September to November) is the best season to travel to Shanghai. 
Summer crowds, the rainy season, and heatwaves begin to fade, prices return to normal, and the weather is perfect for leisurely city walks.
For more stable weather, plan your trip for later than mid-September, and check the forecast before you go. Typhoons can affect Shanghai from July to September, but the probability drops sharply after mid-September.
Beyond weather, if you're hoping to see Shanghai's autumn colors, aim for mid-November to mid-December. Due to global warming, this cooler window has become a more reliable time for foliage.
See more details for traveling in:
Shanghai Weather in September
Shanghai Weather in October
Shanghai Weather in November
Cherry blossoms in full bloom at Guyi Garden in Shanghai in spring
Spring (March to May) is also a great time to visit Shanghai, offering pleasant days around 15°C (59°F) but more light rains (9 rainy days vs. 6 rainy days) compared to autumn.
If you want to experience the traditional Chinese ink painting-like beauty of the water towns, March and April are the best months to visit.
Early to mid-March can be relatively cold, so if you're sensitive to the cold, consider visiting after mid-March.
Late March to early April is the cherry blossom season, where you can enjoy great scenery at spots like Hongkou Football Stadium and Gucun Park.
See more details for traveling in:
Shanghai Weather in March
Shanghai Weather in April
Shanghai Weather in May
5-Day Shanghai and Hangzhou High Tech Tour 
Winter: The Cheapest Time
Lantern Festival at Shanghai City God Temple
Winter (December to February) in Shanghai is cold and damp. It rarely sees snow and mainly experiences rain.
Despite the cold, winter offers two big advantages: costs are generally about 30% lower than normal, and crowds are the thinnest of the year—except around late December (Christmas and New Year celebrations) and early February (Chinese New Year).
Aim for December if winter is your only option, when it is a festive month and the days are not that cold, which means you may still witness Shanghai's beautiful foliage.
As for January and February, the coldest months, it is better to focus on indoor activities with heating, such as admiring ancient bronzes at the Shanghai Museum, marveling at the stunning Jade Buddha at the Jade Buddha Temple, and attending a cooking class in a traditional longtang home.
See more details for traveling in:

Shanghai Weather in January
Shanghai Weather in February
4-Day Shanghai Family Disneyland Tour 
Summer: The Worst Time Without Strategies
Our clients are taking a boat tour in Zhujiajiao Water Town
Summer (June to August) is Shanghai's hottest, rainiest, and most typhoon-prone season, with average monthly rainfall of 5.2 inches and temperatures around 80°F (27°C).
Early to mid-June is your best window, when the temperatures and crowds haven't peaked yet, and rain is less frequent.
July is the hottest and most crowded month. Expect significant increases in hotel and airfare prices, as well as large crowds at attractions.
August is slightly cooler and less crowded than July, but typhoons are more likely and can affect flights. Be sure to check weather forecasts carefully and plan accordingly.
Travel with China Highlights
Even in peak summer, a well-planned trip can still be enjoyable.
We (China Highlights) have designed a series of flexible itineraries that you can enjoy peaceful moments even in the busy season, such as air-conditioned indoor activities, off-peak visits to popular spots like Zhujiajiao Water Town, and a night cruise on the Huangpu River for the stunning view.

If Your Travel Time is Flexible: Dates to Avoid in 2026/2027
For mild weather and fewer crowds, aim for mid-March to late May, or mid-September to mid-November.
To save on rates and avoid the busiest times, try to avoid the peak tourist season (July to August), weekends, and Chinese public holidays.
Chinese New Year: Feb 16－23, 2026 / Feb 5－14, 2027
Labor Day Holiday: May 1－5 (both years)
National Day Holiday: Oct 1－7 (both years)
Still haven't decided how long to spend in Shanghai? Check out our Shanghai Itinerary Guide for inspiration.
Special Note for 2026
The Mid-Autumn Festival holiday (Sep 25－27) falls just three days before the National Day. Domestic travelers are likely to take extra days off to create a longer break.

Top Things to Do in Shanghai: Beyond the Landmarks
 Written by
 Carper
 Updated Aug. 6, 2026 
For first-time visitors, if you only have two or three days in Shanghai, don't try to fit in every famous attraction, but know which experiences are actually worth your time.
Instead of planning Shanghai by the number of places you visit, plan it by experiencing the city's different faces.
Imagine yourself walking through streets shaped by history, tasting flavors that have been part of the city for generations, and ending the day watching the lights from the famous Pudong Skyline.
These moments show why Shanghai is not just another modern metropolis, but one of the most memorable stops on a China journey.
This guide is organised by experiences rather than by attraction popularity, helping you balance Shanghai's historic charm, local life, and futuristic energy without wasting hours on places that may not match your expectations.
What's Actually Worth Your Time in Shanghai
Top Things to Do in Shanghai
How to Prioritize If You Have 1, 2, or 3 Days
FAQs
How to Decide What's Actually Worth Your Time in Shanghai
Shanghai has more attractions and experiences than you could possibly fit into one trip. 
If your time is limited, don't try to check off every famous landmark. Instead, prioritize experiences that help you understand what makes Shanghai unique.
We believe the three experiences most worth your time are its history, its everyday life, and its vision of the future. Together, they show you where Shanghai came from, how it lives today, and where it is heading next.
1. Step Into Shanghai's History, Not Just Its Landmarks
The Bund at night
Shanghai's historic neighborhoods are worth your time because they show you how the city's past still shapes its modern identity. 
Instead of simply ticking off historic buildings as sightseeing stops, walk through neighborhoods where the past is still part of everyday life. 
Old residences sit alongside cafés, local shops, and modern businesses, giving you a chance to experience how Shanghai has evolved without leaving its history behind.
2. Experience How Shanghai Actually Lives
Shanghai local farmers market
To truly experience Shanghai, you don't travel all this way to see how it performs for tourists, but to delve into the city locals actually live in. 
From food and morning markets to neighborhood streets and ordinary daily routines, these experiences help you understand the rhythm, character, and energy of Shanghai in a way that famous attractions alone cannot.
What makes its neighborhoods so special is that none of them feels preserved for tourists; it simply feels lived in.
3. See Shanghai's Leap from Past to Future
Pick up a food delivery brought by a drone.
Shanghai's skyline is worth your time because few places make the city's transformation so visible, both from above and on the river. 
In a single view, you can see the contrast between its historic roots and its futuristic ambitions, giving you a sense of how dramatically the city has changed and how fast it is moving forward.
7-Day Shanghai, Hangzhou and Suzhou Explore the Elegant China
Top Things to Do in Shanghai (Ranked by Experience Value)
Instead of ranking these experiences by how famous the landmarks are, we have ordered them by something more meaningful: the depth of what you actually take away to carry home from each one.
But if you have to pick just two or three, start at the top and work your way down.
1. Walk Along the Bund: See Shanghai's Past and Future Face Each Other
The famous Shanghai skyline
If there is one single spot that justifies the phrase "Shanghai," it is the Bund.  
To get the full effect, the skyline is at its best between 6 PM and 8 PM, when the fading daylight softens the horizon and the new towers begin to sparkle one by one.
Evening is when you will witness the entire riverbank transform into a glowing runway, and the "wow" will remind you why this spot tops our list. But if you want fewer crowds, arrive 30–40 minutes before sunset and stay until the lights come on.
For those who want to explore the Bund in-depth, we recommend a walking tour by day. 
Our guide will walk you through the history of the row of buildings that blend European and Chinese architectural styles and how they survived the war, such as Astor House Hotel, Peace Hotel, and the former HSBC Building.
We are not trying to give you a history lesson, but a chance to see that Shanghai did not erase its past to become modern: it simply built the new by rooting around the old.
If you want to see more aspects of the Bund besides the classic one, combine your Bund walk with a stroll through Waibaidu Bridge to North Bund Green Land, where you find significantly fewer people, unobstructed skyline views, and rewarding scenery along the way.
2. Explore the Former French Concession: Shanghai's Most Walkable Historic Area
The Former French Concession in Shanghai
For visitors who wonder whether Shanghai is nothing but concrete and glass, the Former French Concession tells a different story.
The Former French Concession is at its most lively on weekday mornings (before 9 AM). You'll see locals buying breakfast, walking dogs, opening neighborhood shops, and daily life unfolding beneath the shade of leafy, towering plane trees over quiet, winding streets.
As you wander, keep your eyes open for the old villas with red ceramic roofs and black iron balconies, where elderly residents play chess on folding tables along the streets.
The narrow lilong lanes lead you to hidden courtyards and the tiny cafés that have set up shop in them. Young white-collar workers can always find these quiet hidden gems, enjoy a serene space sipping coffee while tapping on laptops.
If you'd like to explore these quieter lanes without worrying about navigation, our private walking experience combines local food stops with the neighborhood stories most visitors miss.
8-Day Beijing–Xi'an–Shanghai Tour China Golden Triangle
3. Taste Shanghai Through Time-Honored Food and Local Flavors
Shanghai Old Restaurant, one of the most famous local cuisine restaurants in Shanghai.
When you start wondering what you should eat in Shanghai, the real question is often: "What will help me understand this city through its flavors?" Embarking on a Shanghai Benbang food adventure may give you the answer.
Our local food walks focus on carefully selected century-old restaurants still loved by Shanghai locals, rather than tourist-only stops. From Dexingguan and Lao Zheng Xing to other historic eateries, you'll taste each restaurant's signature dish and discover the classic flavors that generations of Shanghai diners have enjoyed.
Feel free to inform your tour guide of your dietary restrictions and allergies in advance so they can make further recommendations. 
However, these famed restaurants generally require you to take a number and wait in line, so it's best to arrive as early as possible during peak meal times to minimize the chance of queuing, such as around 11:00 AM or 5:00 PM.
Want to learn how to cook so you can recreate its delicious flavors at home? Travel with China Highlights, and we'll take you from buying ingredients at a local Shanghai market to visiting a local resident's home in a lilong alley, where you'll quickly learn how to make easy and delicious dishes in a cooking class.
4. See Shanghai from Above: Choose One Skyscraper Experience
Enjoy a panoramic view of Shanghai from the observation deck of the Shanghai Tower.
The city offers multiple observation decks on the skyscrapers, and the choice can easily become overwhelming.
Our advice is simple: if this is your first time in Shanghai, just pick the Shanghai Tower and be done with it.
As the tallest building in China and the third tallest in the world, it gives you the ultimate advantage of looking down on its two famous neighbors—the Oriental Pearl Tower and the Jin Mao Tower—rather than looking up at them from ground level.
The elevator ride to the 118th floor is an experience in itself, and the 360-degree views from the top give you a comprehensive understanding of Shanghai's urban layout.
If watching the sunset above is a must for you, it's recommended that you arrive around 4 PM to avoid long queues that could delay your trip.
For a romantic night, we can help you reserve a dinner on the 119th floor around 6 PM, where you can witness the city light up after the stunning sunset with your loved one.
5. Cruise Huangpu River at Night: See the City Change After Dark
Shanghai Huangpu River Night Cruise
Shanghai feels busy and businesslike during the day, but takes on a completely different personality once the lights come up: more glamorous, more mysterious, and undeniably more romantic.
You can tell the night version of Shanghai feels like a different city altogether. 
As we mentioned, besides taking an evening walk along the Bund and having a romantic dinner on the top of the Shanghai Tower, consider a brief Huangpu River night cruise if you truly want to be surrounded by the spectacle.
Being on a cruise ship means you're surrounded by beautiful scenery, with ever-changing views and a stunning skyline every second. What's more, the cruise ship has a VIP area, which is perfect for those who want to avoid crowds and simply enjoy the scenery in peace.
We suggest taking the classic route, embarking from Shiliupu Marina for about 45 minutes, so you can slow-glide across the water, feel the gentle river breeze, with skyscrapers towering on both sides that no land-based viewpoint can replicate.
For more detailed information, check out: Shanghai Huangpu River Cruise: Route, Price, Tips
How to Prioritize If You Have 1, 2, or 3 Days in Shanghai
The most common mistake travelers make with a Shanghai itinerary is trying to do everything and ending up exhausted without truly experiencing anything. 
Leave your days open for discovery, and engage deeply with each experience.
Haven't decided how many days to stay in Shanghai yet? See our Shanghai Itinerary Planning Guide for your inspiration.
One Day in Shanghai: Sample the Essentials
If you only have 24 hours in Shanghai, your goal should be to feel its most dramatic contrasts in the most efficient way possible.
Morning: Explore the Former French Concession by strolling along the streets lined with leafy plane trees.
Afternoon: Admire the classical Yu Garden for its curved bridges and delicate pavilions. The bazaar outside the garden is also worth your time.
Night: Arrive at the Bund before sunset for the spectacular skyline.
This single day will give you three distinct Shanghais: the elegant, the classical, and the futuristic. All without rushing from one corner of the city to the other.
6-Day Beijing and Shanghai Tour A Tale of Two Cities 
Two Days in Shanghai: Explore by Neighbourhood
With two days, you have the luxury of slowing down and letting each area reveal itself at its own pace. The smartest strategy is to plan your time by neighbourhood, so you are not wasting valuable hours on cross-city commutes.
Explore the Huangpu District from the Bund (1 Day): Visit the old buildings along the Bund promenade, shop at Nanjing Road, wander into the Yu Garden and nearby bazaars, and return to the Bund to witness the dazzling skyline.
Feel Shanghai's Lively Side from the Former French Concession (1 Day): Stroll around the Former French Concession for the shady streets, vintage boutique stores, and tiny cafés at a leisurely pace. Jing'an Temple or Jade Buddha Temple are also optional.
5-Day Shanghai and Hangzhou High Tech Tour 
Three Days in Shanghai: Add a Day in Pudong's Future
Three days allow you to complete the time-travel experience by crossing the Huangpu River and spending a full day in Pudong, the district that represents Shanghai's tomorrow.
Observe the Future Close-Up in Pudong District (1 Day): Peak the Shanghai Tower for the panoramic view of Shanghai city, experience consumer technology at the DJI flagship store, and appreciate the sparkling Lujiazui skyline by taking the Huangpu River night cruise.
Extra Day Options: Time for a Side Trip
Wangxian Valley
If your schedule allows for a fourth day or more, or you simply want to escape the urban intensity, Shanghai offers several compelling options that reward a full day's commitment.
Zhujiajiao or Tongli Water Town: Take a boat tour to glide through its ancient canals, stone bridges, and centuries-old architecture.
Shanghai Disneyland: Perfect for families traveling with kids to enjoy themselves in Asia's biggest Disneyland.
Suzhou: Appreciate classical Chinese gardens while dressing in traditional Han costumes to travel back in time.
Hangzhou: While the West Lake is a must-see for first-timers, Hangzhou cuisine, exemplified by West Lake Fish in Vinegar Sauce, is not to be missed.
Wangxian Valley: It is more like an ancient Chinese theme park than an ancient town, but absolutely worth a night's stay for its stunning night view.
4-Day Shanghai Family Disneyland Tour 
What Is Not Worth Spending Too Much Time On in Shanghai
The fear of wasting time is one of the most common anxieties travelers bring to Shanghai: there is too much for you to see, and not everything deserves your precious hours.
Skip the over-commercialised shopping streets that you can find everywhere. Streets like Nanjing Road are not bad, but if you have limited time, unless you specifically want to buy limited-edition items at certain stores (such as the Pop Mart Global Flagship Store on Nanjing East Road), it's completely skippable.
Visiting more than one observation deck is a classic trap. Aside from the different observation deck heights, the views from the top of Shanghai Tower, Oriental Pearl Tower, and Jin Mao Tower are fundamentally the same. Choose one (preferably Shanghai Tower) and move on; the time you save can be spent in a park or a café where you will actually absorb the city's atmosphere.
Most importantly, stop trying to cover every attraction on your list. Shanghai's true value does not come from checking off landmarks. Allow yourself to pause, to look around, and let the city reveal itself at its own pace.
FAQs
Are there any unusual things to do in Shanghai besides the classical ones?
Shanghai Tian An 1000 Trees
Shanghai Tian An 1000 Trees: You won't regret coming and taking a photo here, as it features over 400 open terraces, each planted with real trees, creating a forest-like appearance that has earned it nicknames like "Shanghai's Hanging Gardens of Babylon" and the "vertical forest".
Shanghai Aurora Art Museum: Unlike the grand Shanghai Museum with its sprawling collections, the Aurora Art Museum is more private and has a stronger design personality. The museum is far less crowded, allowing you to appreciate the exhibits in peace and create a closer connection with your mind.
Shanghai People's Square: Take your time on a weekend morning, and visit a corner of People's Park that transforms into what is known as the "parental dating market". You'll see a side of Shanghai that no guidebook could ever fully capture, where Chinese parents of unmarried adults gather, bringing printed "resumes" of their children and displaying them for blind dates.
Will my kids feel bored in Shanghai? Anywhere else to visit besides Disneyland?
The Shanghai Astronomy Museum
LEGOLAND Shanghai Resort: You and your kids can easily spend 5 hours exploring this LEGOLAND theme park with an average wait time of less than 20 minutes. In contrast, without FastPass, you could wait for hours at Shanghai Disneyland.
The Shanghai Wild Animal Zoo: Great for children who love animals and outdoor exploration. It offers the rare opportunity to observe animals in more natural, open enclosures rather than cramped cages, like giant pandas and red pandas.
The Shanghai Science and Technology Museum: Excellent for curious young minds who enjoy learning about the world through hands-on play. It covers everything from robotics to human biology, and the interactive exhibits keep kids entertained for hours without feeling like schoolwork.
The Shanghai Astronomy Museum: One of the largest and most advanced astronomy museums in the world. Let your children stand on the shoulders of scientific giants and gaze into the cosmos through cutting-edge displays and immersive simulations.
10-Day Leisure River Cruise Getaway TourBeijing - Chongqing - Yangtze River Cruise - Shanghai 
Explore Shanghai with China Highlights
Before you actually set foot on Shanghai soil, what do you hope to gain from this trip?
Well, we would like to show you what we know about Shanghai: the contrast between old streets and modern towers, traditional flavors of centuries-old legacies, lively neighborhoods, and a glowing skyline by the river. 
With the right pace and route, even a short stay can reveal the many sides of this fascinating city.
If you would like to experience Shanghai beyond the typical sightseeing checklist, our local travel experts can help design a private itinerary based on your interests, travel pace, and the way you want to experience China.
